A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same object-orientation generalization study, despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original DNN classification experiments, predictive-model correlations, and robustness evaluations in Section 6 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification and predictive-model results, plus neuron-activation and invariance analyses in Figures 4 and S.7.

M1.justification: v1 Section 4 combines small-angle and in-plane predictors using a maximum and fits parameters by grid search. v2 Section 4.2 adds silhouette-derived predictors, sums four transformed components, and fits logistic and power parameters using gradient descent. These substantially change the predictive model and fitting procedure.

E1.justification: Airplane, car, Shepard-Metzler, and airplane–Shepard-Metzler transfer tasks remain. The lamp dataset evaluated in v1 Appendix C and Figure 20 disappears from v2's reported coverage. v2 still mentions experiments with different object scales generically, so cessation of scale testing is not established, although the earlier specific scenario is no longer documented.

E2.justification: v2 Figures 3b and S.5 add evaluated Random Uniform and In-Distribution null predictors. Comparisons with small-angle, in-plane, and combined predictors remain, now within the revised model evaluation.

E3.justification: v2 Section 4.3 introduces a new penultimate-layer evaluation protocol: activation normalization, model-defined orientation partitions using a 10% threshold at 40 fully-seen instances, and a 95th-percentile activity filter for invariance measurements. Figure 2b also averages accuracy across alpha, whereas v1 Figure 2a displays a fixed-alpha slice. Inception is no longer an experimental architecture.

E4.justification: v2 adds neuronal activation case studies, accuracy–invariance and dissemination analyses, and accuracy comparisons between generalizable and non-generalizable orientations (Figures 4, S.6, S.7). Model ablations additionally examine the contribution of silhouette terms. Earlier detailed Inception, scaling, and lamp robustness results are omitted; several other controls, including half-data experiments, remain.

E5.justification: v1 specifies three trials with 95% confidence intervals, except for cross-category experiments using one trial. v2 Section 4.4 explicitly reports five repetitions per experiment with resampled instance groups. However, v2 does not identify the statistical meaning of its plotted error bars.

E6.justification: v2 reports revised component-model scores and new full-model and null-predictor results; Figure 3b reports full-model correlations above 0.8 across its displayed conditions. Figures 4 and S.7 newly show associations between invariance and partially-seen accuracy, and between fully-seen and partially-seen invariance. Figure S.6 adds partition-specific accuracy results. Earlier Inception, lamp, and scale-specific results disappear. These involve revised predictors and additional analyses, not an established improvement for an unchanged classifier.

T1.justification: v2 adds silhouette-transformed orientation sets and changes the mathematical combination and nonlinear transformation of predictive components. Section 4.3 and Equations 5–8 introduce formal activation averages, an invariance score, activity-based selection, and aggregated network invariance, none of which appears in v1.

C1.justification: v1 principally claims to characterize which unseen orientations DNNs recognize and leaves neural mechanisms for future work. v2's abstract and discussion claim that generalization arises through dissemination of orientation invariance by neurons detecting shared features, making a brain-like mechanism a central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops a shared-feature explanation for transferring invariance and distinguishes successful recognition of fully-seen objects from invariance relative to seed orientations. It interprets failures through absent transferable invariance and adds discussion of temporal association and differences between biological and artificial systems. This substantially extends v1's speculative mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: The data/code statement changes from access upon request to an explicit public repository pointer. Existing classifier hyperparameters, dataset sizes, and hardware details are largely retained and moved into Methods. Conversely, v1's explicit 20-bin discretization and fixed 20% evaluation-instance pool are no longer specified.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the study around mechanisms shared by brains and DNNs. It adds literature on neuronal feature selectivity, biological invariance, and temporal learning, including Desimone et al., Logothetis and Sheinberg, Ruff, and Johnson and Aslin. Earlier dataset-bias and diagnostic-evaluation references, including Torralba and Efros and Hoiem et al., are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and concluding discussion are extensively rewritten. v1's sequential paradigm, visualization, model, setup, and results sections become a Results–Discussion–Methods structure, with appendix implementation material incorporated into Methods. Restricted-seen instances are renamed partially-seen instances throughout.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the paradigm and orientation-cube illustrations, replaces extensive line-plot grids with grouped bar charts, and integrates cross-category comparisons into the main result display. It adds neuron-response image panels and invariance scatterplots and substantially consolidates and replaces the supplementary figures.

improvement.justification: The new activation and invariance measurements give empirical substance to mechanisms that v1 left speculative, while null-predictor controls and increased repetition strengthen the investigation. However, dissemination remains inferred from correlations despite stronger mechanistic claims. Omitted scale, lamp, and Inception analyses narrow robustness evidence, and unspecified error bars reduce statistical transparency. The resulting explanatory gains support a limited overall improvement.
